lead: In 1927 Davisson and Germer fired slow electrons at a nickel crystal and found sharp diffraction peaks at particular angles. Only waves diffract, so the peaks proved that a moving electron carries a matter wave of wavelength λ = h/p. The experiment also separates two speeds of a matter wave: the group velocity, which equals the electron's speed, and the phase velocity, which does not.
prereq: You need: λ = h/p from 6.3, v = ω/k and wave packets from Unit 2, Oscillations and Waves, and Bragg reflection nλ = 2d sin θ from Unit 4, Wave Optics.

sections.h3: The experiment: electrons on a nickel crystal

blocks.text: A particle of momentum p has wavelength λ = h/p. An electron accelerated through 54 V has energy 54 eV and wavelength near 1.7 Å. Atomic planes in a metal crystal are a few ångström apart, so a crystal is a ready-made grating for electrons.

An electron gun heats a filament and accelerates electrons through voltage V, giving each kinetic energy eV. The beam strikes a nickel target. A movable detector records the scattered current versus angle.

At first the current varied smoothly with angle. Then a liquid-air bottle broke, the nickel oxidised, and the target had to be heated for a long time in hydrogen to clean it. That heating also annealed the nickel into large single-crystal regions. The smooth curve became sharp peaks. With 54 V electrons, the strongest peak sat at 50° from the incident beam.

items: A particle bouncing off atoms would scatter broadly and smoothly.
A wave scattered from many parallel planes adds in phase only at certain angles, giving a sharp maximum.
The peak angle moved when the accelerating voltage, hence λ, changed — as a wave picture predicts.

blocks.text: This measured the de Broglie wavelength; it did not merely assume it.

sections.h3: Checking the peak with Bragg's law

blocks.text: A crystal is a set of parallel reflecting planes of spacing d. Waves from successive planes add in phase only when the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths.

blocks.where: n is the order (1, 2, 3 …), λ is the electron wavelength in metres, d is the spacing between neighbouring crystal planes in metres, and θ is the glancing angle between the electron beam and the plane itself (not the normal).

blocks.text: The beam turns through 2θ, so the detector reading is compared with 2θ. For nickel the relevant plane spacing is d = 2.03 Å. The worked example gives 48.55°, within about 3% of the observed 50°.

items: Find the kinetic energy in joules: E = eV.
Find the momentum: p = √(2mE), with m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
Find the wavelength: λ = h/p, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Put n = 1 in nλ = 2d sin θ and solve for sin θ.
Double θ and compare with the measured detector angle.

blocks.text: A pure sine wave has one wavelength and one frequency and travels at the phase velocity vp. A real particle is localised, so its matter wave is a wave packet: many sine waves with wave numbers near a central value k.

blocks.where: ω is the angular frequency in rad/s, k = 2π/λ is the wave number in rad/m, vp is the phase velocity (speed of one crest) and vg is the group velocity (speed of the packet envelope, and hence of the particle). Both are in m/s.

blocks.text: Inside a packet the crests run at vp, but the envelope — the part marking where the particle is — runs at vg. Two waves of nearly equal ω and k give an envelope moving at Δω/Δk, which becomes dω/dk for a narrow spread.

For a matter wave, ω = E/ℏ and k = p/ℏ, where E is total energy, p momentum and ℏ = h/2π. So vp = E/p and vg = dE/dp. For a free particle dE/dp is exactly the particle speed, so vg is the speed of the electron.

In the table v is the particle speed and c is the speed of light. Non-relativistically vp = v/2; relativistically vp = c²/v, which exceeds c. That is allowed, because a pure phase carries no information. The packet moves at vg = v, always below c.

figure.caption: The electron beam, the nickel crystal, the detector and the Bragg check form one chain. The 54 eV beam, the 50° detector reading and the 1.67 Å wavelength are all consistent with each other.

spec.title: Davisson-Germer test
spec.aria: An electron gun sends 54 eV electrons to a nickel crystal, a detector at 50 degrees finds a first-order diffraction peak, and a Bragg check gives wavelength 1.67 angstrom.

examples.question: In a Davisson-Germer set-up, electrons accelerated through 54 V strike a nickel crystal whose reflecting planes are 2.03 Å apart. Find (a) the de Broglie wavelength, (b) the glancing angle θ for the first-order Bragg reflection, and (c) the angle between the incident and diffracted beams. Compare with the observed peak at 50°.
steps: Bragg condition with n = 1: sin θ = λ/(2d) = 1.669 ÷ (2 × 2.03) = 0.4111.
Deviation: 2θ = 48.55°, against 50°. The gap is about 3%, consistent with d being rounded.
For completeness, v = √(2E/m) = 4.36 × 10⁶ m/s, so vg = 4.36 × 10⁶ m/s and vp = 2.18 × 10⁶ m/s.
examples.answer: λ = 1.669 Å, θ = 24.27°, and the diffracted beam is deviated by 2θ = 48.55°, close to the observed 50°.
examples.check:
import math
h = 6.626e-34
m = 9.109e-31
e = 1.602e-19
V = 54
E = V*e
p = math.sqrt(2*m*E)
lam = h/p
print(round(lam*1e10, 3))
d = 2.03e-10
s = lam/(2*d)
print(round(s, 4))
th = math.degrees(math.asin(s))
print(round(th, 2))
print(round(2*th, 2))

examples.question: An electron is accelerated through 100 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength, its speed, and the phase velocity of its matter wave (non-relativistic).
steps: Group velocity equals particle speed: vg = 5.93 × 10⁶ m/s.
examples.check:
import math
h = 6.626e-34
m = 9.109e-31
e = 1.602e-19
V = 100
lam = h/math.sqrt(2*m*V*e)
print(round(lam*1e10, 3))
v = math.sqrt(2*V*e/m)
print(round(v/1e6, 2))
print(round(v/2/1e6, 2))

traps: Writing vg = vp for a matter wave. They are equal only for a non-dispersive wave such as light in vacuum; for a free electron vp = v/2 non-relativistically and c²/v relativistically.
Measuring the Bragg angle from the wrong reference. θ is the glancing angle between beam and crystal plane; the scattered beam turns through 2θ, and the detector reports 2θ.
Using E = 54 eV directly in p = √(2mE). Convert to joules first, or use λ = 12.27/√V Å with V in volts.
Saying the peak proves electrons are particles because they hit the detector. The peak proves they are waves; the detector counts them one at a time.
Assuming the peak angle is fixed. It shifts with accelerating voltage because λ shifts; this voltage dependence is part of the evidence.

quiz.q: State the de Broglie relation used to interpret the Davisson-Germer result, and name the two quantities it connects.
quiz.a: λ = h/p, where λ is the matter wavelength, h is Planck's constant (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) and p is the particle momentum.

quiz.q: Define phase velocity and group velocity of a wave packet.
quiz.a: Phase velocity vp = ω/k is the speed of one crest of a pure sine wave. Group velocity vg = dω/dk is the speed of the packet envelope, hence the speed at which energy and the particle travel.

quiz.q: Why was a nickel crystal used in the Davisson-Germer experiment instead of a metal plate with ordinary scratches?
quiz.a: Diffraction needs scatterer spacing comparable to the wavelength, about 1.7 Å. Only regular atomic planes of a crystal are that close, so they act as the grating; ordinary scratches are thousands of times too wide.

quiz.q: Electrons accelerated through 54 V give a first-order peak at 50°. Using d = 2.03 Å, calculate λ from 2d sin θ and compare with h/p; check consistency with 2θ = 50°.
quiz.a: Take θ = 25°. λ = 2d sin θ = 2 × 2.03 × sin 25° = 1.716 Å. From h/p at 54 eV, λ = 1.669 Å. They differ by about 3%, within the rounding of d, so the Bragg check confirms the de Broglie wavelength.

quiz.q: Show that for a free non-relativistic particle the group velocity of the matter wave equals the particle speed, and find the phase velocity.
quiz.a: ω = E/ℏ and k = p/ℏ, so vg = dω/dk = dE/dp. With E = p²/2m, dE/dp = p/m = v. Then vp = ω/k = E/p = (p²/2m)/p = v/2. The packet moves with the particle; the crests move at half that speed.

quiz.q: Relativistically, the phase velocity of a matter wave exceeds c. Does this break relativity?
quiz.a: No. A pure phase carries no energy or information. The wave packet, carrying the particle's energy and information, moves at vg = dE/dp = pc²/E = v, always below c. Also vp vg = c², so vp > c forces vg < c.

quiz.q: In a wave packet made of waves with wave numbers near k, why does the envelope move at dω/dk?
quiz.a: Two waves with slightly different ω and k add to give a slowly varying factor cos((Δω t − Δk x)/2). A fixed point of the envelope keeps Δω t − Δk x constant, so it moves at x/t = Δω/Δk, which becomes dω/dk as the spread narrows.

beyond: Not for the exam. Low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) and reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) are direct descendants of this experiment and check the atomic layout of crystal surfaces during thin-film growth. Electron microscopes at 100–300 kV use electron wavelengths of a few picometres, which is why they can resolve atoms. Electron cryo-microscopy used exactly this wave behaviour to map protein structures. The group velocity idea reappears in optical fibres as group velocity dispersion, which limits how far a pulse travels before it smears out.
